title: Adding without double counting
objectives: Use inclusion and exclusion for two and three events.
Spot an overlap counted twice, and a sum above 1 as its warning sign.

screens.title: Counted twice
screens.prose: Draw one card from a standard deck. 13 cards are hearts and 12 are face cards: jacks, queens and kings. Each number counts the cards in its region.
screens.question: A friend says $13 + 12 = 25$ cards are a heart or a face card. Tap the region the friend counted twice.

hints.text: Which cards are in the 13 and also in the 12?
The middle region holds cards that belong to both circles.
The jack, queen and king of hearts are hearts and face cards. Both counts include them.

feedback.correct: The jack, queen and king of hearts sit in both counts.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the cards that are in the 13 hearts and also in the 12 face cards.

byKey.A: Those 10 hearts are not face cards. They are in the 13 only, so they were counted once.
byKey.B: Those 9 face cards are not hearts. They are in the 12 only, so they were counted once.
byKey.none: Those 30 cards are in neither count. The friend left them out, and rightly so.

explain.text: The 13 hearts include the 3 heart face cards, and so do the 12 face cards. Adding 13 and 12 counts those 3 cards twice. The true count is $10 + 3 + 9 = 22$.

screens.prose: Now build the event “a heart or a face card” yourself. A card counts if it is a heart, a face card, or both.

state.caption: Tap a region to select it, tap again to clear it

screens.question: Tap every region whose cards are a heart or a face card.

hints.text: Does a heart that is not a face card count?
Three regions sit inside at least one circle.
Take the hearts only, the overlap and the face cards only. Leave the outside alone.

feedback.correct: Three regions: 10, 3 and 9 cards, each card counted once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take every card inside at least one circle.

byKey.and-only: You took only the cards that are both. “Or” also takes cards that are just one of the two.
byKey.everything: The 30 cards outside both circles are neither a heart nor a face card.
byKey.none: The 30 cards outside both circles are neither a heart nor a face card.
byKey.A: The 10 hearts that are not face cards still count. A heart is enough.
byKey.B: The 9 face cards that are not hearts still count. A face card is enough.
byKey.AB: The 3 heart face cards count too. “Or” includes both.

explain.text: Your three regions hold $10 + 3 + 9 = 22$ cards. Each card is counted once, because the regions do not overlap. That is $25 - 3$: the friend's total minus the cards counted twice.

screens.prose: Your regions form the **union** $H \cup F$, read “$H$ or $F$”. The overlap is the **intersection** $H \cap F$, read “$H$ and $F$”. Adding the two counts takes the intersection twice, so we take it away once.
screens.question: What is $P(H \cup F)$, the chance one card drawn is a heart or a face card?

widget.label: Chance of a heart or a face card

hints.text: How many of the 52 cards are in the union?
You counted them on the last screen.
22 of the 52 equally likely cards are a heart or a face card. Divide 22 by 52.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cards in the union once each, then divide by 52.

byKey.added: You used 25 cards: $13 + 12$. The 3 heart face cards were counted twice.
byKey.twice: You took the 3 shared cards away twice, leaving 19. Take them away once.
byKey.both: That is the intersection, cards that are both. The union also has cards that are only one.
byKey.count: 22 is the number of cards. The chance is that count out of 52.

explain.text: We counted $13 + 12 - 3 = 22$ cards, so $P(H \cup F) = \tfrac{22}{52} = \tfrac{11}{26} \approx 0.4231$. Dividing each count by 52 gives the same sum in chances: $\tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{12}{52} - \tfrac{3}{52}$.

screens.prose: Now chances instead of counts. Roll two fair dice. $A$ is “the first die shows 6” and $B$ is “the second die shows 6”. Each has chance $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

state.caption: Only the overlap is filled in

screens.question: What is $P(A \cup B)$, the chance of at least one six?

widget.label: Chance of at least one six

hints.text: Which roll is in both $A$ and $B$?
The double six is in both events. Its chance is $\tfrac{1}{36}$.
Add $\tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{1}{6}$, then take away $\tfrac{1}{36}$ once for the double six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two chances, then take the overlap away once.

byKey.added: You added $\tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{1}{6}$. The double six is in both, so it was counted twice.
byKey.twice: You took $\tfrac{1}{36}$ away twice, so the double six is not counted at all.
byKey.both: That is the chance of a double six, the intersection. You want at least one six.

explain.text: You added $\tfrac{6}{36} + \tfrac{6}{36}$ and removed the double six once: $\tfrac{11}{36}$. The complement agrees: no six has chance $\tfrac{25}{36}$, and $1 - \tfrac{25}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$.

screens.prose: Back to one card. This time $H$ is “a heart” and $S$ is “a spade”.

state.caption: No card is in the overlap

screens.question: What is $P(H \cup S)$?

options.why: You took $\tfrac{1}{52}$ away for an overlap. No card is a heart and a spade, so nothing was counted twice.
You multiplied the two chances. That would be a chance of both, and one card cannot be both.
That is the chance of a heart alone. A spade also counts.

hints.text: How many cards are both a heart and a spade?
The overlap holds 0 cards.
With nothing counted twice, add: $\tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{13}{52}$.

feedback.correct: 26 of 52 cards: the overlap is empty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cards in the overlap first.

byKey.ghost: You took $\tfrac{1}{52}$ away for an overlap. No card is a heart and a spade, so nothing was counted twice.

explain.text: No card is both a heart and a spade, so $P(H \cap S) = 0$. Events like these are **disjoint**, and the rule becomes plain addition. $\tfrac{13}{52} + \tfrac{13}{52} - 0 = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

screens.prose: Roll a fair die. $A$ is “at most 4”, so $P(A) = \tfrac{4}{6}$. $B$ is “even”, so $P(B) = \tfrac{3}{6}$. The regions show the faces.
screens.question: What is $P(A \cup B)$?

options.why: You added the two chances and got more than 1. That is the giveaway: 2 and 4 were counted twice.
You capped the sum at 1. The face 5 is in neither event, so the union misses it.
You took the overlap away twice. Take $\tfrac{2}{6}$ away once.

hints.text: Can any chance be bigger than 1?
Faces 2 and 4 are in both events.
$\tfrac{4}{6} + \tfrac{3}{6} - \tfrac{2}{6}$. Or count the faces inside the circles.

feedback.correct: Five faces, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, are in the union.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chances, then take the overlap away once.

byKey.added: You added the two chances and got more than 1. That is the giveaway: 2 and 4 were counted twice.
byKey.capped: You capped the sum at 1. The face 5 is in neither event, so the union misses it.

explain.text: Adding gives $\tfrac{7}{6}$, which no chance can be. The faces 2 and 4 sit in both events, so take $\tfrac{2}{6}$ away once. That leaves $\tfrac{5}{6}$: every face but 5.

screens.title: Three events
screens.prose: With three events we add $|A| + |B| + |C|$, subtract the three pair overlaps, then add the triple overlap. Follow one card from a shaded region through each step.

state.caption: One card in $A$ and $B$ only; one card in all three

screens.question: Fill in how many times each card is counted. Net is the first count, minus the pairs, plus the triple.

hints.text: A card in all three circles is in $A$, in $B$ and in $C$. How many of the three counts include it?
A card in all three is in every pair overlap: $A \cap B$, $A \cap C$ and $B \cap C$.
All three: counted 3 times, subtracted 3 times, added back once, net 1. $A$ and $B$ only: 2, minus 1, plus 0, net 1.

feedback.correct: Every card in the union ends up counted exactly once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each card, count how many of the terms contain it.

byKey.r1c2: A card in $A$ and $B$ but not $C$ is in one pair overlap, $A \cap B$, only.
byKey.r1c4: Net is $2 - 1 + 0$. Check the pair column first.
byKey.r2c1: A card in all three is in $A$, in $B$ and in $C$: three counts.
byKey.r2c2: A card in all three is in all three pair overlaps, so it is subtracted 3 times.
byKey.r2c3: The triple term counts the cards in $A \cap B \cap C$ once.
byKey.r2c4: Net is $3 - 3 + 1$. Without the triple term the card would vanish.

explain.text: Each row nets to 1, so every card in the union is counted once. The triple region is the delicate one: in 3 times, out 3 times, so the last term puts it back. That is why the signs alternate.

screens.prose: Your counts give the rule of **inclusion and exclusion**. Add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple. $$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$$ $$\begin{aligned} P(A \cup B \cup C) = {} & P(A) + P(B) + P(C) \\ & - P(A \cap B) - P(A \cap C) - P(B \cap C) \\ & + P(A \cap B \cap C) \end{aligned}$$

state.caption: A stock screen with three filters

screens.question: Of 100 stocks, 40 pass momentum, 35 value and 30 quality. The pairs pass together 12, 10 and 8 times. Five pass all three. How many pass at least one?

widget.label: Stocks passing at least one filter

hints.text: Start with $40 + 35 + 30$.
Subtract the three pair counts, then add the triple once.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the singles, subtract the pairs, add the triple.

byKey.added: You added the three filters. Stocks passing two or three filters were counted more than once.
byKey.no-triple: You stopped after the pairs. The 5 stocks passing all three were then removed completely; add them back.
byKey.minus-triple: You subtracted the triple. The signs alternate: the triple is added back.

explain.text: $40 + 35 + 30 - 12 - 10 - 8 + 5 = 80$. The diagram now shows each region; they add to 80 inside the circles. The other 20 stocks pass no filter.

screens.prose: A trend signal looks at a stock's close against two moving averages. Over its history the close is above the 50-day average on 60% of days. It is above the 200-day average on 50%, and above both on 45%.
screens.question: On a random day, what is the chance the close is above at least one of the two averages?

widget.label: Chance above at least one average

hints.text: What happens if you simply add 0.6 and 0.5?
The 45% of days above both averages are in both numbers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two chances, then take away the days above both once.

byKey.added: You added 0.6 and 0.5 and got more than 1. The days above both averages were counted twice.
byKey.one-only: That is the chance of being above exactly one average. Days above both also count.
byKey.both: That is the chance of being above both. “At least one” is bigger.
byKey.neither: That is the chance of being above neither: $1 - 0.65$.

explain.text: $0.6 + 0.5 - 0.45 = 0.65$. The regions show it: 0.15 above the 50-day only, 0.45 above both, 0.05 above the 200-day only. The close sits below both averages on the other 35% of days.

screens.prose: A desk has three risk limits, and bad days breach several at once. Limits 1, 2 and 3 are breached on 10%, 8% and 5% of days. Pairs 1 and 2, 1 and 3, 2 and 3 are breached together on 4%, 3% and 2%. All three on 1%.

state.caption: Breaches tend to come together on bad days

screens.question: What is the chance at least one limit is breached on a given day?

widget.label: Chance at least one limit is breached

hints.text: Subtract the three pairs, $0.04 + 0.03 + 0.02$, then deal with the triple.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Singles, minus pairs, plus the triple.

byKey.added: You added the three limits. Days that breach two or three limits were counted more than once.
byKey.no-triple: You stopped after the pairs. Days that breach all three were then removed completely; add them back.
byKey.minus-triple: You subtracted the triple. Its sign is plus.

explain.text: $0.10 + 0.08 + 0.05 - 0.04 - 0.03 - 0.02 + 0.01 = 0.15$. The seven regions inside the circles add to 0.15 too. Because breaches cluster, the risk is well below the 0.23 a naive sum suggests.

ideas: Adding two counts takes the overlap twice, so take it away once.
For three events: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triple. Every outcome then counts once.
Disjoint events have no overlap, so their chances simply add.

formula.name: Inclusion and exclusion
formula.tex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
formula.note: For disjoint events the last term is 0.

summary.trap: Adding the chances of overlapping events counts the overlap twice. A total above 1 is the giveaway.

quiz.prose: Two events have $P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(B) = 0.4$. You are told $P(A \cup B) = 0.7$.
quiz.question: What is $P(A \cap B)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rearrange $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.

byKey.sum: You added $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. The overlap is how far that sum overshoots the union.
byKey.a-only: You worked out $0.7 - 0.4$, the chance of $A$ without $B$. The overlap is the rest of $A$.
byKey.gap: You subtracted $0.4$ from $0.5$. The union is needed to find the overlap.

explain.text: Rearranging the rule gives $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$. That is $0.9 - 0.7 = 0.2$: the plain sum overshoots the union by exactly the overlap.

quiz.prose: A whole number from 1 to 100 is picked at random, each equally likely.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is divisible by 2 or by 5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count multiples of 2, of 5, and of both.

byKey.added: You added 50 and 20. The 10 multiples of 10 were counted twice.
byKey.twice: You took the 10 multiples of 10 away twice. Take them away once.
byKey.both: That is the chance of being divisible by both, that is by 10.

explain.text: There are 50 even numbers and 20 multiples of 5. The 10 multiples of 10 are in both counts. So $50 + 20 - 10 = 60$, and the chance is $0.6$.

quiz.prose: A whole number from 1 to 30 is picked at random, each equally likely.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is divisible by 2, 3 or 5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Singles, minus pairs, plus the triple.

byKey.added: You added 15, 10 and 6 and got more than 30 numbers. Multiples of 6, 10 and 15 were counted twice or more.
byKey.no-triple: You stopped after the pairs. The number 30 was then removed completely; add it back.
byKey.minus-triple: You subtracted the triple. Its sign is plus.

explain.text: Singles: 15 multiples of 2, 10 of 3, 6 of 5. Pairs: 5 multiples of 6, 3 of 10, 2 of 15. The triple is 30 alone, so $31 - 10 + 1 = 22$ and the chance is $\tfrac{11}{15}$.

quiz.prose: Two events have $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.6$. Nothing else is known.
quiz.question: What is the smallest $P(A \cap B)$ can be?

options.why: You let the events be disjoint. Then $P(A \cup B)$ would be $1.3$, above 1.
You multiplied the chances, which assumes independence. Nothing says they are independent.
That is the largest the overlap can be, when $B$ sits inside $A$.

feedback.correct: The union can be at most 1, so the overlap is at least $1.3 - 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P(A \cup B) \le 1$ in the rule.

explain.text: The rule gives $P(A \cap B) = 1.3 - P(A \cup B)$. The union is at most 1, so the overlap is at least $0.3$. Two likely events must overlap.
